replies.text: the number is never as useful as what you do after seeing it. i've learned to decide the next action before i check anything. what's the first thing you're changing based on this?
i feel like half of these scores look scary but don't actually move anything. are you going to act on it or is it just fun to screenshot?
ok now i'm curious, what did you check that gave you this result? and did it match what you expected?
in practice the painful part isn't picking the db, it's re-embedding everything when you swap models. interviews rarely cover that. is reindexing one of your 20?
i'd add a question on when you don't need a vector db at all. a lot of apps are fine with pgvector. does your list cover that tradeoff?
saving this for later. which of the 20 do candidates flub most often in your experience?
big prompts only pay off overnight when success is checkable. vague goal plus a long run gives you a confident wrong pile at 8am. do you make the agent run tests before it stops?
big prompts feel productive but i'd bet the morning review is where the time goes. is reading the output eating the time you saved?
waking up to finished work sounds amazing. what's the most surprising thing an agent got done for you overnight?
docs rot silently. a broken quickstart costs more than a bad landing page because the dev who bounces never tells you. which blocker does your agent hit the most so far?
the real test is a clean machine with zero context, which is exactly what new users have. does the agent get to google when stuck or does it have to stay inside the docs?
the isolated cloud computer per run is a neat touch. have you pointed it at any big devtool docs yet, and which one had the most broken steps?
month resets feel arbitrary but they work. i like picking one thing to finish per month and ignoring the rest. what's the one thing you want to get done this october?
a rough last october doesn't predict much, it's mostly a good excuse for a fresh start. what would make this one a clear win for you?
fingers crossed for you. what happened last october that you're hoping doesn't repeat?
in recruiting the hard part usually isn't matching, it's trust in the data and getting hiring managers to actually use the tool. are you tackling sourcing or screening first?
i'd also talk to recruiters who hate their ATS, they'll show you the real workflow fast. what are you hoping to learn from builders specifically?
talent tech feels like it's about to change a lot. what got you into this space?
i think founders lose clarity before they lose the will. when you can't tell which thing moves the needle, effort starts to feel pointless. what do you do on the days your will runs low?
pushing harder every hour is also how people burn out before the real problem shows up. staying in the game long enough matters too. where do you draw the line between pushing and burning out?
what made you land on will as the number one reason? was it something you lived through yourself?
rock-hard in the middle is basically every v1 i've ever shipped. looks done, isn't. do you fix it with a longer cook or just start over?
two minutes is the lie, instant noodles always under-promise on timing. is three minutes your sweet spot?
midnight project syncs sound rough. what are you working on that keeps landing at midnight?
new chapters tend to sneak up while you're busy building. sounds like a good month is ahead. what are you most excited to share first when you can?
keeping a little mystery before the reveal is a good move. do you find the build up makes announcements land better?
congrats in advance, sounds like something exciting is coming. what's the dream you've been building toward the longest?
the red flags often show in how they talk about their other founders, not just how they treat you. what was the first red flag you noticed in a meeting?
you can feel it fast, but i'd still ask 2 or 3 of their portfolio founders before taking a check. do you do reference calls on investors too?
sounds like this comes from a meeting that went sideways. what was the moment that gave it away?
timelines like this are confusing since administrative steps and criminal outcomes can run on separate tracks. which part of the process is least clear to you?
worth remembering the two processes don't always move in the same order, so it can look odd from outside. have you followed a case like this before?
sounds like a complicated situation. which part of how it's unfolding are you following most closely?
agent infra gets scary once agents hold secrets. scoped, short-lived credentials matter more than which model you pick. what's the most common way you see teams leak keys to agents?
secure by default beats secure with a good guide, since most builders won't read the guide. what's one default you wish every agent framework shipped with?
i'm in sf so this is on my radar. what's the main thing you want people to walk away with from your talk?
for me personal brand on x came more from replying consistently than from posting. replies are where people actually meet you. what's the one habit that grew yours the most?
i'd argue showing up in other people's replies matters more than any community. who are you most hoping to connect with, founders or creators?
what does the community actually do day to day? is it mostly feedback on posts or accountability?
i keep learning the hard way that some jobs are worth handing to pros. echoing across three prefectures is a good reminder. what made you grab the mic in the first place?
echoing across prefectures is kind of a flex though, that's reach. was it intentional or a total accident?
wait, where was this? were you announcing something?
the fix is boring: a merge-field check before send. one unfilled variable and you've told the whole inbox that nobody read it. which tool do you think caused this one?
a qa agent is a real idea, but pretending to be an investor is a trust burn no checker fixes. would you pay for a tool that just blocks the send?
'hello First Name Last Name' is a classic. what's the best cold email you've ever received?
when the pool is that big, deciding your 3 criteria before looking at anyone helps a lot. otherwise you end up picking whoever you saw last. what's the first filter you're using to cut it down?
15k sounds huge but i'd guess the top 50 are obvious on the first pass. the hard part is the messy middle. are you scoring everyone or going with your gut at the end?
lock in energy, i'm into it. what's the thing you're choosing one for?
recruiting events work best when people can actually talk about the work, not just collect swag. happy hour is a good format for that. are you doing short intros or just open mingling?
recruiting over drinks is underrated. people are way more honest about what they want than in an interview. do you usually get more senior folks or early career ones at these?
SF tech week is going to be packed, nice timing. which role at micro1 are you most excited to fill?
launch videos get the views, but the how-to video is what turns them into actual users. views and activation are different games. did the 100K turn into signups yet?
the explainer after the launch is the smart move. attention fades fast if people don't know what to do next. which video is converting better so far?
congrats on 100K! what was in the first 3 seconds of the launch video that made people stay?
summarizing the log is the easy part. the useful part is knowing which node failed and what data went into it. would the tool pull in the failing node's input too?
i'd want it to go past summary and suggest a fix. 'node 4 failed' is meh, 'your api key expired' is gold. are you planning read-only or would it retry things too?
not just you, error logs are the worst part of automation. which n8n error has annoyed you the most recently?
most of these tools can write a decent email. lead quality and filtering is where they differ, so i'd test that first. what's the ICP you're testing them on?
friendly warning: they all look great in demos and reply rates tell the real story. i'd run the same batch of leads through each one. how are you planning to compare them?
following this one. what's the thing you want from an outbound tool that you haven't found yet?
community spaces survive when the money side is boring and steady. day passes covering rent is a smart way to keep it affordable. are most of the day passes booked by students or locals?
this is the kind of use case where a platform makes sense: the host has the mission, the platform handles the revenue. how do hosts usually get their first few bookings?
a place in berkeley where students actually feel they belong is so needed. what kind of events has the space hosted so far?
the posts that stick with me are the ones that change what i build next, usually something obvious that nobody acts on. has this one changed anything you're working on?
depends a lot on stage though. what works at 10 users often breaks at 10k. what stage were you thinking about when you posted this?
okay now i'm curious. what sparked this for you today?
designers from those teams know real design systems but still want ownership, which is a good fit for startups. what do founders get most wrong when hiring their first designer?
contract or part time is often a better first step for early teams. you get taste without the full commitment. are you seeing more founders go that route lately?
useful offer for founders. what do the designers you know stand out at most, product, brand or motion?

public deadlines work best when the scope is small enough to actually finish. a small thing shipped beats a big thing half done. what's yours, and what's the smallest version you could ship next week?
public commitment helps, but 'before november' is vague. i'd add an exact date to make it real. what's the day you're shipping?
okay this got me thinking about my own list. what's yours, and which item on it scares you the most?
every startup has at least one silicon valley scene happening somewhere, usually the pivot or the demo going wrong. which episode feels most accurate to you right now?
the show was almost too accurate, now the real thing just moves faster. hot take: the AI era would be a better season than crypto was. which character would the timeline be?
lol what's on your timeline today that set this off?
waiting on something to finally land always feels longer than it actually was. how long had this been on your list?
okay but did it live up to the wait? sometimes the finally is better than the thing itself. how does it feel now that it's here?
can't tell what the finally is and now i'm very curious. what were you waiting on?
posting burnout is real. batching content in one sitting and scheduling it helped me more than forcing daily posts. how often are you posting right now?
breaks are healthy, but on X consistency matters. i'd cut frequency instead of stopping fully. how long are you planning to step away?
enjoy the break! what's the first thing you're going to do with the extra time?
the safest pattern i've seen is agents getting scoped, short lived tokens while a separate service does the actual signing. how do you handle revocation when a token leaks?
keys out of context helps, but a tricked agent can still ask the signer to sign something bad. so you need limits on what it can sign. do you enforce policies at the signer?
this is a real problem for anyone building agents. how are you solving it at 1Claw, a vault the agent calls or a proxy?
from the founder side, a preempt saves months of raising, which is time back for building. the tradeoff is less time to compare terms. what do you need to see on the first call to move that fast?
preempting works when the founder has momentum, but it can also push people to decide too quickly. where do you draw the line between conviction and rushing?
what's the signal that makes you preempt instead of waiting for the round to form?
from the builder side i just hope it doesn't distract from the products themselves. a lot of us depend on these tools every day. which part of it are you watching most closely?
big personalities, big stakes. i'd rather watch what ships than the back and forth. is there a part of this you think actually matters for builders?
i haven't followed it closely. what's the main thing they're disagreeing about right now?

in a contest like this the hard part is making the metric legible to normal people. 'biological age' needs a one line explanation or the results get ignored. how do you explain what an aging clock actually measures?

i think the most interesting outcome is where the clocks disagree with each other. a head to head only works if people trust the ground truth. what's the tiebreaker when two clocks give opposite answers?
a six month contest with this many labs sounds like a logistics beast. what's been the hardest part to coordinate so far?

same pattern shows up all over infra: access gets abstracted into a rental, and the constraint moves from availability to price. then it's about who can afford the lease. does that make enforcement easier or harder?
pricing problem is a good frame, but a lease is also way easier to monitor than a chip sitting in a warehouse. could be a loophole or a chokepoint. which way do you think it goes?
where do you track deal level stuff like compute leases? is there a source you trust for it?
as a young builder the first job is getting strangers to care in one sentence. waterloo already has a lot of builder energy to work with. what's the first problem in the city you'd fix?
most prosperous city in the world is a big claim, which works as a rallying line. what's the one metric you'd use to know waterloo is getting there?
good luck with the run Jerry. what made you decide to jump in now instead of waiting a few years?

design engineer roles are where the product gets its feel, and with voice there's no UI to hide behind. the tradeoff is speed vs polish in states like listening and thinking. which state is hardest to get right?
voice first products still need good visual feedback. people trust what they can see it hearing. do you think the best voice product ends up mostly invisible or mostly visual?
owning everything from data model to final pixel sounds fun. what does the first month look like for whoever gets this role?
every time i set up storage and permissions i end up in five tabs just to make one bucket readable. simplicity mostly lives in the defaults. which aws service needs it most?
aws simplified usually just means a new service on top of the old ones lol. the real fix is fewer concepts, not another console. what's the one thing you'd delete if you could?
ok this feels like it comes from a real fight. which service broke you this time?
the boring fix that works is scoped, short lived creds per task, so the agent never sees the real prod key. most of the pain is setting it up once. how do you give your agents access right now?
a sandbox with prod keys is just an incident with extra steps. the credentials have to live inside the sandbox boundary too, not just the code. have you seen a team actually do this right?
painfully accurate lol. what's the closest call you've seen with an agent holding real keys?
ha, the best dreams come true because someone shipped the thing nobody else wanted to build. what did Igor originally ask for?
now the real test is whether igor uses it every week or just posts about it. what's your bet?
ok i need context here 😄 what was the dream?
libraries that stick usually nail the first five minutes: one install, one example that actually runs. docs matter more than features early. what's the first example someone sees in yours?
python is the right call if devs are the audience, but distribution is the hard part, not the code. how are you planning to find your first 100 users?
i can't see much from the link. what problem made you build this library?
.com wins on trust when someone googles you cold, but .ai reads as a signal in AI and is easier to get. it's brand clarity vs availability. which did you end up picking for yours?
.io and .ai feel like a small credibility tax long term, most people still type .com by default. early on nobody cares though. would you buy the .com later?
is this for a real startup or just curiosity? which one are you leaning toward right now?
scoped and revocable is the right default. the part teams skip is expiry: a key that dies when the task ends beats one someone has to remember to rotate. how short do you set the default ttl?

scoping helps, but an injected prompt can still use whatever the agent is allowed to do. so limits on amounts and actions matter as much as the key. do you enforce spending caps at the credential layer?
how does revocation work when an agent is mid task? does it fail gracefully or just break?
i only trust the model that wins on my own tasks over a week. switching costs are mostly prompts and evals anyway. what task did you test it on first?
one benchmark chart rarely survives real workloads, especially long agent runs where reliability beats peak score. did you run it on anything beyond the standard evals?
is this the launch chart or your own testing? what's the first thing you'd throw at it?
custom ui skills are underrated. encoding spacing and type rules once saves so many back and forth prompts. the tradeoff is they go stale as the design moves. how do you keep them updated?
the skills probably matter more than the model here, since taste lives in the constraints. would it look this good with a different model and the same skills?
this looks clean. what's the one rule in those ui skills that changed the output the most?

the specificity is what makes it work. geese around the ring road beats 'nature' every time. same in marketing, tiny concrete details carry more than any big claim. which of these is your strongest memory?
backrooms but warm is a fun flip, the genre is usually about dread. this one is nostalgia that still feels liminal. is the emptiness part of the comfort for you?
plov, manti and samsa in one sentence is dangerous. which dish do you miss most?
the connect posts that work are the ones where people drop what they're building, not just hi. gives others something to reply to. what are you building right now?
tag lists like this get a lot of 'hi' and few real convos. one specific problem you're stuck on would pull better people. what's the one you're stuck on this week?
solo founder plus agentic loops is a fun combo. what's the agent you're building at the moment?
in my experience the human feel comes from the inputs, real details and quotes, way more than the prompt. the model just assembles. what do you feed it before it writes?
99% human on a detector isn't the same as readers feeling it's human. voice and weird specific details do that. have you tested the output on real readers?
sounds like a cool pipeline. which manual step would you most want to automate first?
1.2M views rarely turns into followers unless the reel makes people want the next one. hook gets the view, series gets the follow. did the reel have a clear reason to follow, or was it a one off?
reels and ads do different jobs though. reels are lottery tickets, ads are repeatable. i'd put a small budget behind the reel that already won. have you tried boosting this one?
that's a big reel. what was in the first 2 seconds, a face, text on screen or a b-roll shot?
depends who wrote the tests. if the same model wrote code and tests, they just agree with each other. i'd hand-write the edge cases first. do you review the tests as hard as the code?
passing tests only proves what you thought to test. the scary stuff is auth, perf and weird inputs nobody specced. i'd ship it behind a flag first. would you go straight to prod or canary it?
curious where your line is. a small util, sure, but payments or auth code? what's the riskiest thing you've actually shipped from AI output?

teleop data is the bottleneck in robotics and gamers already have the reflexes, so this makes sense. same pattern everywhere in AI, data quality beats volume. is the player driving a real robot or a sim?
cool idea but the sim to real gap is the catch. games forgive physics that real objects don't. i'd guess the value is in intent, not exact motion. do you think it works for fine grip tasks?
wait is the person playing actually controlling a real robot somewhere? how do they handle the lag?
from the founder side, a double reschedule is usually chaos, not disinterest. a short async message with one concrete question often gets answers when calls don't. would you try one more async nudge?
i'd give it one more nudge before writing it off. early founders flake on anything that isn't revenue or fundraising that week. what's your cutoff, two nudges or three?
that's annoying. what did you want to chat with them about, investing, a collab or something else?
sharing got way easier for me once i stopped treating it as marketing and just posted what we shipped that week. way easier to keep up. what are you building during these 30 days?
length of time matters less than replies imo. a few months of replying to people beats a year of only posting into the void. are you doing mostly posts or replies in this 30 day run?
day 5 already, nice. what made you start the 30 day challenge now?
x clout is distribution, not value. a real product with zero audience still works, the audience just makes early customers cheaper to find. who was the buyer here, the team or the product?
fun stat but small sample. clout doesn't matter much for acqui-hires, it matters when you're the one trying to sell. was this about the team or the tech?
ok this is wild. what did the 68 follower company actually build?
the best founder news is usually a customer renewing or paying without being chased. nothing beats that feeling. what was the moment this one started to feel real for you?
plot twist, the best news is also the start of a harder phase. the week after a win is when i see people get the most distracted. what's the first thing you're doing with it?
congrats! now i need the details 👀 what's the story behind it?

classic fast path bug: the cheap check ran on the placeholder, not the payload. same class of bug shows up in media pipelines when metadata says small and the file is huge. how did you spot it was the short pages failing?
i'd add an assertion on real size right before the embedding call, not only upstream. fast paths lie quietly. do you log chunk sizes after chunking now?
the detail that the failing pages were the short ones is such a good clue. was the content lazy loaded or injected by JS?
pre big day nerves are real. i've learned to finish the boring prep early so the last days are just excitement. what's the one thing still left on your list?
honestly the countdown is the best part, the anticipation sometimes beats the day itself. do you plan the whole thing out or just wing it?
ooh what's happening in 5 sleeps?
portfolio wins, but a live thing with real users beats a polished case study. even a few users says more than a readme. what's the best portfolio piece you've seen lately?
partly true, but distribution still isn't level. a great portfolio nobody sees doesn't help. you have to put it where hiring people actually look. where do you think that is?
did you hire or get hired off a portfolio instead of a resume? what was the project that convinced you?
building in public plus vibe coding is a good combo, your shipping log basically becomes your portfolio. what are you building right now?
people connect faster over one concrete project than a list of interests. pick the one you're most into and post a thing about it. which one is it for you?
vibe coding and building in public is my zone too. what's the last thing you vibe coded?
a cracked team early on is mostly about who ships without being asked. what's the one habit that made your team work like that?
cracked is fun but the real test is how a team handles a bad week. the good ones stay fast when stuff breaks. what was the hardest week at Finc so far?
what is Finc building right now? curious what the team is shipping.
a marketplace listing is distribution you don't have to build, but only if the integration works in about 5 minutes. people drop fast otherwise. what's the review process like for getting listed?
nice, but a directory listing only works if docs and first run are clean. otherwise it's just another logo wall. are you looking for APIs or full apps?
this sounds useful. what kind of services are getting listed so far?
ai builders and vibecoders is a good crowd to be around. the fastest way i've found to connect is replying to what people ship. what are you building at the moment?
a list of interests is hard to reply to. one concrete thing you're working on gets way more people saying hi. what's the project you'd lead with?
ai builders and crypto is an interesting mix. which side are you more into right now?
a bare link gives people no reason to click. a one line result you got for a client does a lot more. what's the one outcome you're proudest of?
link only posts are tough on X, the algo and people both tend to skip them. say who you help and what changed. who's your ideal client?
what kind of brands do you usually work with?

with site-to-reel the content is the easy part. the hard part is pacing, a reel needs a hook in the first 2 seconds and site copy doesn't give you that. did you have to prompt for the hook or did it land on its own?
three iterations is the real flex, most people quit after one mid output. i'd bet the website as source of truth did more work than the model. did you give it any brand constraints up front?
this looks clean. is Flow 2.0 something you're shipping to customers or an internal tool? and what did you point Claude at first, the homepage or the docs?

classic local-run energy. what saves me on long jobs is chunking them so a crash or a thermal nap doesn't cost the whole run. is this running locally on purpose or are you testing before moving it to a server?
the 1h 25m nap is your laptop telling you it's done being a prototype machine. great for testing, bad for anything sustained. what's the plan once it works, keep it local?
ok now i need to know what's cooking. model, build, render, something else? what are you making?

with files the scary part isn't the model, it's not knowing where the bytes went. making the route visible before the run is the right fix. do you show it on every run or only when the choice changes?
visible choice is good but it only works if the default is safe, most people never flip a toggle. is On this Mac the default in Flow or does the user pick every time?
reading the route before you run is a clean mental model. does the local model's draft hold up for real client work or do people still bounce to cloud for the final pass?

people reply when they see their own current project in your post. a list of 12 topics gives them nothing to grab. i'm building in ai tooling in SF so agents and dev tools is my overlap. what are you shipping right now?
12 topics is a lot for the algorithm and for humans to place you. pick the two you'd talk about for hours and lead with those. which two would it be for you?
indie hacking plus ai agents is a fun combo. are you building an agent product right now or mostly using agents to ship your own stuff faster?

more thinking budget can mean the model argues itself out of a right first answer. on coding tasks that shows up as overengineering or rewriting stuff that already worked. have you seen that in your own agent runs?
also benchmarks are noisy. a small gap between max and xhigh could just be variance, especially if it's a few runs each. did Anthropic say how many samples they averaged per setting?
not a dumb question, it's the one a lot of people are wondering. in your own coding work do you default to the highest setting or step it down for most tasks?
what changed most is that the build step got so cheap. the hard part now is getting anyone to care once it's live, distribution is the real bottleneck. what are you building at the moment?
most exciting and also most crowded. shipping is cheap now so taste and distribution are the only moats left. which one are you betting on?
what's the one thing you're building right now that wouldn't have been possible a year ago?
a bare link is a gamble for the reader. if this is something you made, the line that gets clicks is the one saying who it's for. who is it for?
friendly tip: add one line of context next to the link. people click way more when they know what they're getting. so what's behind this one?
no context in the post so i'm curious. is this something you built or something you found? what's the story behind it?
staged rollouts are rough for builders, you can't plan around a model you can't call. that's why i keep the model behind a swappable layer. are you waiting on api access or app access?
a model you can't use doesn't change anything yet, launch day threads are mostly vibes. i'd wait for real usage reports. what would make you actually switch to it?
'excellent reading assignment' got me lol. did your access come through since you posted, and if so what's the first thing you tested?

onboarding that asks for a new habit loses, onboarding that rides an existing one wins. otp autofill inside the gmail habit is exactly that. did installing the extension feel like friction or was it worth it?
smart, but an extension install is still a big ask for a new product. it only works if the payoff is instant. did the code autofill right on your first login?
autofilling otps from email is such a small thing that kills a big annoyance. what is Avec exactly and how did you find it?
when output gets cheaper the bar goes up, not the free time. building anything now means shipping 3x the scope because you can. do you feel it more at your job or on side projects?
i'd say it's less 10x work and more 10x scope. hours stayed the same, ambition grew. is the extra load stuff you chose or stuff people now expect from you?
what's one task AI made way faster for you that got replaced by even more work?
gccs keep going up in Hyderabad, and it deepens the talent pool but also makes hiring tougher for smaller companies there. do you think it helps or hurts startups in the city?
a gcc usually means real engineering ownership moves closer to the product, not just support work. that's the bigger shift. do you know which teams DoorDash is starting with?
congrats to everyone there! do you know what the first hires will be, backend, ml or ops?
keeping the source next to the claim is the right unit of trust, reviewers hate hunting for it. how does Flow handle a figure when the source is a messy pdf table?
25 of 25 matching is great, but i'd want to see what a mismatch looks like. does Flow flag it before the human review or only show the proof beside it?
a fictional campaign is a smart way to demo this without client data. how did you design it so the numbers still felt realistic?
diffs you can review beat a clean output you can't explain, that's what makes agents trustworthy long term. do you store the history per document or as one project log?
agents will change, yes, but the real lock-in risk is the format the record lives in. plain files you can move beat any clever store. is the record in an open format or Flow-specific?
'a place to come home' is a nice way to frame document edits. what does the review step look like when an agent rewrites a whole section?
'it's all still your code' is the line that matters, visual builders usually lose devs at the export step. how clean is the output when someone drags a form onto the canvas?
drawing outside the breakpoints is a bold choice, most builders box you in there. does it generate separate responsive rules or does the css get messy fast?
congrats on 1.1! an agent chat built for midcode sounds fun. what's the first thing people usually ask it to do?
works for marketing too. 'what do you do today instead' shows the real competitor, usually a spreadsheet or doing nothing. what's the most surprising workaround you've heard from a user?
good question, but i'd add how often the workaround actually hurts. a rare annoying hack isn't worth building for. how do you decide when a workaround is painful enough?
have you put that question directly in a feature request form, and did people actually answer it?
in-house creators only work if they're allowed to post like creators. once legal reviews every cut it's just a slower ad team. have you seen a big brand actually give them that freedom?
or it means ads stopped working and they finally noticed. hiring is the easy part, trusting a creator inside a big company is the hard one. which old brand do you think is doing it best?
which brand was this? curious if they hired one face or built a whole little studio inside. which setup do you think holds up longer?
small team rituals like snack runs end up mattering more than fancy perks. cheapest morale tool there is. what snack disappears first at your place?
the real startup stack is a snack spreadsheet. what's your system, one giant bulk order or splitting it across a few stores?
ok but what are you guys building at autumn these days? curious what the team is heads down on right now
roadmaps like this usually skip the boring part: evals and getting something in front of real users. that taught me more than another course. which step do people underestimate most?
friendly pushback: i'd build one small thing end to end first and fill in theory when you hit a wall. do you think the order really matters or can people jump around?
did you put this together from your own path into LLM engineering? which part was the hardest to learn on your own?
a consistent visual vibe does more for recognition than any tagline, same in marketing. how do you decide what stays fixed across your pieces?
with stuff like this the vibe is the product and community does the rest. do you think bored ape style projects still have that pull or has it moved somewhere else?
what's the story behind this one? was it a mood you wanted first or a concept you built around?
hiding pricing can boost inquiries but it filters out people who just want to self-serve. a rough range plus a form worked better in my experience. what's your inquiry to call rate looking like?
pushback: removing pricing adds friction for buyers who'd have said yes fast. would you test it against a version with a 'starting at' price?
